frameworks.name: Deal Variable Multiplication Framework
frameworks.definition: A negotiation approach that breaks an offer into multiple independent dimensions (price, speed, ease, risk) to expand trading leverage while maintaining reciprocity.

frameworks.name: Value Equation Framework
frameworks.definition: A model organizing all variables in a transaction into four axes: speed (timeline), risk (who bears responsibility), ease (friction), and price, enabling flexible concessions without eroding value.

frameworks.name: ROI Framing vs. Cost Framing
frameworks.definition: A persuasion technique that repositions an expenditure from a cost center (overhead, expense) to an investment center (return-generating asset), increasing buyer conviction.

claims.text: Reciprocity only matters in cultures where reciprocity is a norm; in cultures where reciprocity is not valued, people exploit systems designed around reciprocal exchange (Alex Hormozi). This cultural mismatch occurs when people from non-reciprocal cultures interact with reciprocal-exchange systems and perceive them as naive rather than obligating.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Culture values reciprocity as a norm
Interaction between two cultural groups with different reciprocity norms
claims.mechanism: In cultures without reciprocity norms, explicit value exchanges are perceived as one-way gifts rather than obligating transactions.
bounded_by: Does not apply to non-reciprocal cultures
Breaks down when cultural assumptions mismatch

claims.text: The difficulty in reciprocal negotiation is not recognizing that an exchange occurred, but assessing whether the traded concessions are equal in perceived value (Alex Hormozi). A small favor (bringing lunch to a table) and a large request (airport pickup) both trigger reciprocity feeling, but the value differential makes the trade unfair.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: People track reciprocal exchanges emotionally and notice when something was given, but struggle to calibrate relative value accurately.

claims.text: To stay in favorable reciprocity during negotiation, break each major offer into as many independent variables as possible, so you have more trading dimensions to work with (Alex Hormozi). A $15M house deal can be decomposed into: cash vs. financed, 30-day vs. 90-day close, furnished vs. unfurnished, reducing reliance on price-only concessions.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Multiplying variables gives the negotiator more arrows in the quiver; concessions on non-price dimensions preserve price integrity while satisfying reciprocity.
bounded_by: Does not apply to commodities with fixed terms
Requires flexibility in the underlying transaction

claims.text: The four core value-equation variables in any transaction are: (1) speed (timeline to delivery/completion), (2) risk (who bears costs if things go wrong), (3) ease (friction or convenience for the buyer), and (4) price (monetary cost). Skilled negotiators manipulate all four, not just price.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Anchoring strategy in negotiation works by presenting an initial high anchor in the opening offer, then making counter-offers that appear to move significantly downward while introducing multiple simultaneous offers that preserve the seller's core position (Alex Hormozi). The psychological effect: the buyer feels they are winning concessions across multiple dimensions, lowering their anchor expectations.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Multiple simultaneous offers presented or available
Initial anchor is significantly higher than target price
claims.mechanism: High initial anchor shifts the buyer's reference point; subsequent concessions on variables other than price create the perception of winning without eroding the seller's profitability.

claims.text: By maintaining reciprocity across five value variables (speed, risk, ease, price, and other deal terms) instead of two, a negotiator can concede on one dimension and gain movement on another, staying at approximately the same target price while increasing buyer satisfaction (Alex Hormozi). Example: offer 15M at stated price, then add 'ease' to drop buyer's counter from 17M to 16M, then add 'risk' to drop further to 15.5M, then add 'speed' to reach target.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Multiple variables available for flexible negotiation
claims.mechanism: Multiplying trade dimensions makes concessions feel substantial (reciprocally balanced) while preserving the core financial outcome.

claims.text: Framing fundamentally changes buyer perception and willingness to accept an offer; most buyers do not understand framing and will accept the frame the seller presents without question (Alex Hormozi). For example, 'This costs $5,000' vs. 'A $5,000 investment yields $15,000 in maintenance cost savings' present the same financial reality but trigger different buyer mental models.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Buyer is unfamiliar with framing tactics
claims.mechanism: Buyers unconsciously anchor to the frame presented by the seller, interpreting the same offer as either an expense (cost center, overhead) or return-generating asset (investment), changing perceived ROI.

claims.text: When selling an employee or vendor offering to a buyer, reframe the transaction as an investment with expected ROI rather than as a cost or overhead line item (Alex Hormozi). An employee should pitch: 'Investing in me means you get a percentage commission on revenue I bring in' rather than 'I cost you $X/year,' inverting the buyer's cost-benefit mental model.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Transaction is employee or vendor offering
Buyer treats standard offerings as cost centers
claims.mechanism: Reframing from cost to investment shifts the buyer's decision gate from 'can we afford this?' to 'what is our expected ROI?'
bounded_by: Does not eliminate cost-center perception in all contexts
Requires credible ROI data to be effective

claims.text: As a buyer, reframe the seller's offer in the opposite direction—as cost or overhead—to increase negotiating leverage, because pushing the seller down and pulling yourself up (by reframing) asymmetrically favors the buyer (Alex Hormozi). Simultaneously, present your own offer using investment framing, creating frame asymmetry.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Operating as a buyer in a negotiation
Seller has presented their offer using positive framing
claims.mechanism: Frame asymmetry creates psychological leverage: you perceive the seller's offer as low-value overhead while positioning your counter-offer as high-value investment.

claims.text: For home-improvement sales, use comparative neighborhood data and resale value impact to reframe cost as an investment; a $100,000 pool that adds $200,000 in home resale value is not a $100,000 cost but a $100,000 investment with a 2x return (Alex Hormozi). This reframing is stronger than the alternative: 'Your house is worth $1M; comparable homes with pools sell for $1.2M; this pool costs $100K but adds $200K in value.'
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Home improvement or real estate transaction
Resale value data is available and favorable
claims.mechanism: Anchoring the buyer's cost perception to neighborhood comps and resale multiples reframes the purchase as capital deployment with measurable returns, not consumption.
bounded_by: Does not work if homes with/without the feature sell at similar prices
Buyer skepticism can override frame if data is weak

claims.text: When selling home improvements, frame the conversation using actual comparable sales data from the neighborhood, showing homes that sold with vs. without the feature, and quantifying the price differential or resale premium (Alex Hormozi). This data-backed framing is more persuasive than abstract claims of value.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Comparative data grounds the frame in observable reality, reducing buyer skepticism and reframing the investment as market-validated rather than seller-biased.
bounded_by: Data must be recent and specific to the neighborhood
Weak or contradictory data undermines the frame

claims.text: High-ticket deal negotiators should develop a comprehensive deal sheet tracking 80+ variables they can adjust (Alex Hormozi), enabling them to enter negotiations with maximum flexibility and stay in reciprocity while making favorable trades on price and terms.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Multiple variables available in the deal structure
claims.mechanism: Having 80 variables at disposal means the negotiator can concede visibly on several without eroding core financial position, satisfying reciprocity while staying on target price.

examples.text: In a real estate transaction, a buyer offers $17M for a $15M house. The seller concedes on 'ease' (handling closing logistics, reducing buyer friction), and the buyer drops their counter to $16M. The seller then concedes on 'risk' (accepting more liability for certain contingencies), and the buyer drops further to $15.5M. Finally, the seller concedes on 'speed' (accelerating the closing timeline), and the buyer accepts $15M—the seller's target price. Throughout the sequence, the buyer feels they are winning concessions (reciprocity is satisfied), but the seller preserves the core price by trading on multiple variables.

A home services contractor (pool, patio, awnings business) frames a $100,000 pool installation differently to buyers: Rather than saying 'This costs $100,000,' they present neighborhood comps showing that homes with pools sell for $1.2M versus $1.0M without pools (a $200,000 premium). The framed pitch: 'A $100,000 pool investment adds $200,000 in home value. You get to enjoy the pool the entire time you live here, and it costs half the actual value it adds when you sell.' This reframing shifts the buyer's decision from 'Can we afford a $100K expense?' to 'Is this a good capital deployment?'

An employee interviewing for a role pitches themselves as an investment rather than a cost: 'I'm not a $60,000/year salary expense; I'm a percentage-commission investment that generates revenue ROI. The business only pays if I bring in results.' This reframes the employer's decision gate from cost-center budgeting to return-on-investment thinking.

When a vendor presents a service as a $5,000 investment that generates $15,000 in measurable maintenance cost savings, the buyer perceives it differently than the same vendor saying 'This service costs $5,000.' The identical financial reality is reframed from overhead (cost-center thinking) to capital deployment (investment thinking).

practices.text: Before entering a negotiation, map all available deal variables (timeline, risk allocation, delivery speed, payment terms, scope flexibility, contingencies, etc.) so you have maximum flexibility when trading concessions.
When presenting a buyer offer or seller proposal, lead with the investment framing or return metrics rather than the cost or price alone.
Anchor high in initial offers and anchor low in counter-offers, using multiple simultaneous offers to create flexibility in concession-making while preserving core price targets.
For home-improvement or real-estate sales, gather neighborhood comparables data showing resale value impact before pitching to frame the expense as a market-backed investment.
